planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; this old European selection is grown for its flowers rather than fruit.

directions: Plena is a long-grown European elder selection whose yellow stamens convert into extra petals, turning the usual flat, lacy elder bloom into a fully double, creamy-white cluster. Because the flowers are the whole point, prune lightly right after bloom rather than hard in late winter, removing only crossing or dead wood so next year's flowering wood is preserved. It still sets some small black fruit after flowering, but cropping is sparse and the shrub is best treated as an ornamental specimen in a mixed border. Give it the same moist, fertile soil and full sun to light shade that any elder prefers, and expect a looser, more open habit than fruiting cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; interplanting a second elderberry cultivar nearby typically improves cropping.

directions: Samnor is a vigorous Danish commercial black elderberry bred for heavy fruit set, producing large, flat flower umbels that ripen into dense clusters of small black berries. Growers commonly interplant a second nigra cultivar to boost yields, and the resulting harvest is typically processed into syrup, cordial, or wine rather than eaten fresh. Renewal-prune each dormant season by removing the oldest, least productive canes at the base while keeping one- and two-year wood, which carries most of the following season's bloom. As with all elderberry, cook the fruit before use and discard stems and leaves, which are not edible.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, fertile soil; this heirloom color-break selection is grown mainly as a curiosity and ornamental accent.

directions: Fructu Luteo is an old European elder sport grown for berries that ripen amber-yellow instead of the usual glossy black, making it a conversation piece in a mixed fruit planting or hedgerow. Growth habit, flower timing, and cultural needs otherwise track the wild species closely, so it tolerates the same range of soils and benefits from the same periodic removal of old canes to keep fresh fruiting wood coming. The yellow fruit is used the same way as black elderberry, cooked into syrup or jelly, though some growers simply let it stand as an ornamental substitute for black-fruited forms. Because birds find the pale berries less obvious than black ones, netting may extend how long the crop stays on the bush.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring alongside a compatible late-flowering cultivar; Giant's Heart ripens notably later than most honeyberries and needs cross-pollination to fruit.

directions: Giant's Heart is a patented Berries Unlimited introduction bred in the late-ripening Blue Treasure group, carrying noticeably larger, heart-shaped berries than early Russian and Saskatchewan selections. Because it blooms and fruits later in the season, pair it with another late-flowering honeyberry so bloom windows overlap, rather than with the earliest pollinizer cultivars. The bush is cold-hardy and otherwise managed like other haskaps, needing minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood once established. Its later ripening window helps extend the honeyberry harvest after earlier cultivars have already finished.

planting.note: Plant with a different honeyberry cultivar nearby for cross-pollination; Cinderella ripens early to mid-season.

directions: Cinderella is a honeyberry valued for large, sweet blue fruit, ripening among the earliest to mid-season fruits of the garden year. Like nearly all haskap selections it is self-incompatible, so a second, overlapping-bloom cultivar must be planted within pollinator range for it to set a worthwhile crop. The compact bush tolerates extreme winter cold and late spring frosts during bloom, making it a reliable choice for northern plantings where many other fruiting shrubs struggle. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing deadwood, since fruit forms mainly on second-year and older canes.

planting.note: Plant with a different, overlapping-bloom honeyberry cultivar for pollination; Rebecca is a late-ripening Polish selection.

directions: Rebecca is a Polish-bred honeyberry that ripens its blue fruit later in the season than many of the Siberian and Saskatchewan-derived cultivars. Yields are reported as notably heavy for the species, so a sturdy support or open spacing helps keep heavily laden branches from sprawling. As with all haskap, it needs a cross-pollinating partner with an overlapping bloom period to set fruit reliably. Culture otherwise follows standard honeyberry practice: full sun, consistently moist slightly acidic soil, and light annual thinning of old wood rather than hard pruning.

planting.note: Plant alongside another early-blooming honeyberry cultivar for pollination; Blue Horn is a vigorous, upright Russian selection.

directions: Blue Horn is a Russian honeyberry selection noted for an unusually vigorous, upright growth habit and large fruit compared with many compact haskap cultivars. Like all haskaps it is self-incompatible and depends on overlapping bloom with a compatible pollinizer cultivar to set a worthwhile crop. The taller, more open framework benefits from slightly wider spacing than dwarf honeyberry types so light reaches the lower canopy. Otherwise it is managed like other haskaps: full sun, evenly moist slightly acidic soil, and light removal of old or crossing wood rather than heavy annual pruning.

planting.note: Plant with another early-blooming honeyberry cultivar for cross-pollination; Blue Moose is grown primarily for its own heavy fruit production.

directions: Blue Moose is grown chiefly for its own exceptionally heavy crop of large blue berries, which can turn an entire bush blue at peak ripeness. Like all haskap selections it is self-incompatible, so planting a second, overlapping-bloom cultivar nearby is necessary for reliable fruit set. Culture follows standard honeyberry practice: full sun, moist slightly acidic soil, and minimal pruning limited to deadwood and crossing branches. Because flowers open very early, siting away from the most frost-prone low spots in the garden helps protect bloom from a late cold snap.

planting.note: Plant with another early-blooming honeyberry cultivar for cross-pollination; Smokey Blue is an early-flowering selection named for its powder-blue fruit.

directions: Smokey Blue takes its name from the matte, powder-blue bloom on its berry skin, which gives the fruit a frosted look distinct from the glossier dark blue of many other honeyberry cultivars. It flowers early in the season, so it should be paired with another early-blooming cultivar to ensure overlapping bloom and reliable cross-pollination, since haskaps are largely self-incompatible. Like other members of the species, the bush is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates late frosts during bloom better than most fruiting shrubs. Keep pruning light, removing only dead or crossing wood, since fruit is borne on second-year and older canes.
